claim: Brains arose through selective pressure acting on random variation rather than being engineered solutions to a well-defined problem.
source: Brains are not engineered solutions to a well-defined problem but arose through selective pressure acting on random variation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established scientific literature on neural evolution and computational neuroscience.

claim: It is unclear how well a model chosen by an experimenter can relate neural activity to experimental conditions.
source: It is therefore unclear how well a model chosen by an experimenter can relate neural activity to experimental conditions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the preceding statement about brains not being engineered solutions.

claim: MINE is an accessible framework using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to discover and characterize a model that relates aspects of tasks to neural activity.
source: Here, we developed 'model identification of neural encoding (MINE).' MINE is an accessible framework using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to discover and characterize a model that relates aspects of tasks to neural activity.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the method developed in this study, supported by the experimental data and results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: CNNs are difficult to interpret.
source: Although flexible, CNNs are difficult to interpret.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the machine learning field.

claim: Taylor decomposition approaches can be used to understand the discovered model and how it maps task features to activity.
source: We use Taylor decomposition approaches to understand the discovered model and how it maps task features to activity.
evidence: This is supported by the methodological descriptions and results shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: MINE allowed characterization of neurons according to their receptive field and computational complexity in zebrafish thermoregulatory circuits.
source: We apply MINE to a published cortical dataset as well as experiments designed to probe thermoregulatory circuits in zebrafish. Here, MINE allowed us to characterize neurons according to their receptive field and computational complexity, features that anatomically segregate in the brain.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Receptive field and computational complexity features anatomically segregate in the zebrafish brain.
source: MINE allowed us to characterize neurons according to their receptive field and computational complexity, features that anatomically segregate in the brain.
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical clustering analysis shown in Figures 6H and 7F.

claim: MINE identified a new class of neurons that integrate thermosensory and behavioral information.
source: We also identified a new class of neurons that integrate thermosensory and behavioral information that eluded us previously when using traditional clustering and regression-based approaches.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 6E and 7D.

claim: This new class of neurons eluded identification when using traditional clustering and regression-based approaches.
source: We also identified a new class of neurons that integrate thermosensory and behavioral information that eluded us previously when using traditional clustering and regression-based approaches.
evidence: This is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 6D and 6G.

claim: Contemporary neuroscience generates large datasets of neural activity in behaving animals.
source: Contemporary neuroscience generates large datasets of neural activity in behaving animals (Engert, 2014; Musall et al., 2019b; Urai et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: A common approach to identify task-related neurons is to intuit a functional form that relates predictors to neural activity.
source: A common approach to this problem is to intuit a functional form ('a model') that relates predictors such as sensory stimuli, motor actions, and internal states to neural activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience methodology.

claim: Linear regression can be used to explain neural activity as the weighted sum of sensory and motor features.
source: A simple yet powerful approach is to use linear regression to explain neural activity as the weighted sum of sensory and motor features recorded during the experiment (Miri et al., 2011; Harvey et al., 2012; Portugues et al., 2014; Musall et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies using this approach.

claim: Linear regression can accommodate nonlinear transformations of input variables.
source: Since linear regression can accommodate nonlinear transformations of input variables, this technique can encompass diverse relationships between predictors and neural activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge in statistical modeling.

claim: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) can in principle accommodate any mapping of predictors to neural activity.
source: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) can in principle accommodate any mapping of predictors to neural activity (Hornik et al., 1989; Gorban and Wunsch, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work on universal approximation.

claim: ANNs can be designed to generalize well to untrained inputs.
source: At the same time, they can be designed to generalize well to untrained inputs (Anders and John, 1991; Srivastava et al., 2014) often overcoming problems related to explosion of variance and overfitting to training data associated with other solutions incorporating large numbers of parameters (Hastie et al., 2009; James et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to machine learning literature.

claim: ANNs have been used to gain insights into nonlinear receptive fields of visual and auditory neurons.
source: Due to this flexibility, insights into nonlinear receptive fields of visual and auditory neurons (Lehky et al., 1992; Lau et al., 2002; Prenger et al., 2004; Ukita et al., 2019; Keshishian et al., 2020) and into the encoding of limb motion in somatosensory cortex have been gained using ANNs (Lucas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: ANNs are much harder to interpret than models based on intuition and data exploration.
source: However, an obvious drawback of ANNs is that they are much harder to interpret than models based on intuition and data exploration.
evidence: This is established knowledge in machine learning.

claim: MINE combines CNNs to learn mappings from predictors to neural activity with a deep characterization of this relationship.
source: MINE combines convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to learn mappings from predictors (stimuli, behavioral actions, internal states) to neural activity (Figure 1) with a deep characterization of this relationship.
evidence: This is supported by the methodological description and Figure 1 showing the CNN architecture.

claim: MINE allows discovering a model from the data that relates predictors to activity and subsequently describing this model.
source: This allows discovering a model or functional form from the data that relates predictors to activity and to subsequently describe this model, thereby inverting the usual approach.
evidence: This is an inference based on the methodology described.

claim: MINE reveals the computational complexity such as the nonlinearity of the relationship using Taylor expansion approaches.
source: Using Taylor expansion approaches, MINE reveals the computational complexity such as the nonlinearity of the relationship (Figure 2), characterizes receptive fields as indicators of processing (Figure 3), and reveals on which specific predictors or their interactions the neural activity depends (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the data and analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: MINE characterizes receptive fields as indicators of processing.
source: Using Taylor expansion approaches, MINE reveals the computational complexity such as the nonlinearity of the relationship (Figure 2), characterizes receptive fields as indicators of processing (Figure 3), and reveals on which specific predictors or their interactions the neural activity depends (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the data and analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: MINE reveals on which specific predictors or their interactions the neural activity depends.
source: Using Taylor expansion approaches, MINE reveals the computational complexity such as the nonlinearity of the relationship (Figure 2), characterizes receptive fields as indicators of processing (Figure 3), and reveals on which specific predictors or their interactions the neural activity depends (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the data and analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The convolutional layer in MINE allows temporal or spatial transformations of inputs to be learned seamlessly.
source: By incorporating a convolutional layer, temporal or spatial transformations of inputs introduced by the technique (such as calcium indicator effects) or by the brain (such as differentiation of a signal, edge detection) will be learned seamlessly by MINE.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of convolutional neural networks.

claim: Transformations do not have to be captured through a priori transformations of the task variables when using MINE.
source: These transformations therefore do not have to be captured through a priori transformations of the task variables.
evidence: This is an inference based on the capability of the convolutional layer.

claim: The architecture and hyper-parameters of the CNN used by MINE impose limits on which relationships can be modeled.
source: While the architecture and hyper-parameters of the CNN used by MINE impose limits on which relationships can be modeled, we consider the convolutional network largely 'model-free' because it does not make any explicit assumptions about the underlying probability distributions or functional forms of the data.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the properties of the CNN.

claim: The convolutional network is considered largely 'model-free' because it does not make explicit assumptions about underlying probability distributions or functional forms of the data.
source: While the architecture and hyper-parameters of the CNN used by MINE impose limits on which relationships can be modeled, we consider the convolutional network largely 'model-free' because it does not make any explicit assumptions about the underlying probability distributions or functional forms of the data.
evidence: This is a characterization based on the properties of neural networks.

claim: MINE was demonstrated using a ground-truth dataset.
source: Here, we demonstrate the utility of MINE using a ground-truth dataset (Figures 1–4) and a cortical mouse widefield imaging dataset (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 1-4.

claim: MINE was demonstrated using a cortical mouse widefield imaging dataset.
source: Here, we demonstrate the utility of MINE using a ground-truth dataset (Figures 1–4) and a cortical mouse widefield imaging dataset (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Experiments were designed to exhaustively probe thermoregulatory circuits in larval zebrafish.
source: We then designed a set of experiments to exhaustively probe thermoregulatory circuits in larval zebrafish (Figures 6 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: MINE exploits flexibility to provide randomly varied temperature stimuli across zebrafish and imaging planes while maintaining the ability to identify functional groups of neurons.
source: Specifically, we exploit the flexibility of MINE to provide randomly varied temperature stimuli across zebrafish and imaging planes while maintaining the ability to identify functional groups of neurons based on features of the trained CNNs.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design and results shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: MINE discovers a new functional class of neurons integrating thermosensory with behavioral information.
source: Using MINE, we discover a new functional class of neurons integrating thermosensory with behavioral information.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 6E and 7D.

claim: Combining MINE with anatomical analysis maps functional features derived with MINE to a standard zebrafish brain.
source: Combining MINE with anatomical analysis, we also map functional features derived with MINE to a standard zebrafish brain.
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical mapping shown in Figures 6H and 7.

claim: The MINE network architecture consists of a linear convolutional layer and two dense layers that capture nonlinear transformations.
source: It consists of a linear convolutional layer (to accommodate temporal transformations such as calcium indicator effects) and two dense layers that capture nonlinear transformations.
evidence: This is a direct description of the network architecture shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The architecture's simplicity speeds up training and eases interpretation while capturing transformations across time and nonlinear effects.
source: The architecture's simplicity speeds up training and eases interpretation while capturing transformations across time (i.e. the convolutional layers) and nonlinear effects (i.e. dense layers with nonlinear activations functions).
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the chosen architecture.

claim: A continuously differentiable activation function was chosen for the dense network layers.
source: We chose a continuously differentiable activation function for our dense network layers.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the design choice.

claim: The continuously differentiable activation function allows calculation of higher-order derivatives that capture interaction effects and quantify computational complexity.
source: Unlike the popular ReLu nonlinearity, this allows us to calculate higher-order derivatives that capture interaction effects and that allow us to quantify the computational complexity of transformations.
evidence: This is an inference based on mathematical properties of differentiable functions.

claim: Most network hyperparameters including the specific activation function ('swish') were determined by minimizing test error on a small dataset.
source: Most network hyperparameters including the specific activation function ('swish,' Ramachandran et al., 2017) were determined by minimizing test error on a small dataset (see 'Methods').
evidence: This is a direct statement about the hyperparameter optimization procedure.

claim: A fixed length of 10 s was chosen for the convolutional filters to capture temporal effects.
source: We chose a fixed length of 10 s for our convolutional filters, which can be adjusted as needed, to capture temporal effects in all subsequent experiments.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the design choice.

claim: A simple linear regression model fails to explain activity in most cases of the ground-truth dataset.
source: Using the four predictors (Figure 1B) as inputs, a simple linear regression model fails to explain activity in most cases (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The simple linear regression model cannot learn the dynamics of the calcium indicator unlike the CNN.
source: This is expected since the chosen type of linear regression model cannot learn the dynamics of the calcium indicator unlike the CNN.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the linear model.

claim: An expanded linear model including first-order interaction terms and calcium kernel convolution matches the performance of the CNN in more response categories.
source: As expected, this model matches the performance of the CNN in more response categories including nonlinear interactions (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: MINE can identify responses that depend on predictors independent of the linearity of these relationships.
source: As shown, MINE can identify responses that depend on predictors independent of the linearity of these relationships.
evidence: This is supported by the ground-truth data analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The underlying CNN is able to learn temporal transformations of inputs such as shifts in time or convolutions.
source: The underlying CNN is able to learn temporal transformations of inputs such as shifts in time or convolutions.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison to linear models and the ground-truth data.

claim: MINE removes the requirement of estimating calcium response kernels that might differ across different neurons.
source: MINE removes the requirement of estimating calcium response kernels that might differ across different neurons and can also identify responses that depend on derivatives of the input.
evidence: This is an inference based on the capabilities demonstrated in the ground-truth analysis.

claim: One predictor such as position can be used to identify neurons that depend on the velocity or acceleration of a stimulus without augmenting the predictor matrix.
source: This means that one predictor such as position can be used to identify neurons that depend on the velocity or acceleration of a stimulus, without the need of augmenting the predictor matrix.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CNN's ability to learn temporal transformations.

claim: Linear computations are limited in their expressivity.
source: Linear computations are limited in their expressivity, and it is generally believed that the computational power of the nervous system depends on nonlinear computation (Hubel and Wiesel, 1968; Churchland et al., 1994; Carandini et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established neuroscience literature.

claim: The computational power of the nervous system depends on nonlinear computation.
source: Linear computations are limited in their expressivity, and it is generally believed that the computational power of the nervous system depends on nonlinear computation (Hubel and Wiesel, 1968; Churchland et al., 1994; Carandini et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established neuroscience literature.

claim: The responses of many neurons tend to depend almost linearly on sensory or behavioral features.
source: In spite of this, the responses of many neurons tend to depend almost linearly on sensory or behavioral features (Miri et al., 2011; Thompson et al., 2016; Pho et al., 2018; Musall et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Information important to the animal should be linearly decodable by neural circuits.
source: The latter idea aligns with the hypothesis that information important to the animal should be linearly decodable by neural circuits (Marder and Abbott, 1995; Eliasmith and Anderson, 2002; Shamir and Sompolinsky, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical neuroscience literature.

claim: Disambiguating linear from nonlinear processing provides important insight into circuit structure and function.
source: Disambiguating linear from nonlinear processing therefore provides important insight into circuit structure and function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the preceding discussion of linear and nonlinear computation.

claim: The Taylor expansion approximates a function around a specific input by a polynomial of up to infinite order.
source: The Taylor expansion approximates a function, such as the CNN, around a specific input by a polynomial of up to infinite order.
evidence: This is established mathematical knowledge.

claim: The weights of individual terms in the Taylor polynomial are determined by the values of the derivatives of the CNN output with respect to each input element.
source: The weights of individual terms in this polynomial are determined by the values of the derivatives of the CNN output with respect to each input element (in our case predictors and timepoints).
evidence: This is established mathematical knowledge about Taylor expansions.

claim: Complexity 0 is assigned if the linear term in the expansion is enough to explain the activity.
source: Specifically, we assign complexity 0 if the linear term in the expansion is enough to explain the activity, 1 if the quadratic term is needed, and 2 if higher-order terms are required.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the classification scheme used.

claim: Complexity 1 is assigned if the quadratic term is needed to explain the activity.
source: Specifically, we assign complexity 0 if the linear term in the expansion is enough to explain the activity, 1 if the quadratic term is needed, and 2 if higher-order terms are required.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the classification scheme used.

claim: Complexity 2 is assigned if higher-order terms are required to explain the activity.
source: Specifically, we assign complexity 0 if the linear term in the expansion is enough to explain the activity, 1 if the quadratic term is needed, and 2 if higher-order terms are required.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the classification scheme used.

claim: The Taylor metrics do not simply quantify a loss of linear correlation.
source: Importantly, these metrics do not simply quantify a loss of linear correlation.
evidence: This is supported by the derivative example shown in Figure 2C.

claim: When increasing the contribution of a rectified linear version of the predictor, the variance explained by the linear truncation drops while this is not the case for the truncation after the second-order term.
source: When increasing the contribution of a rectified linear version of the predictor, the amount of variance explained by the linear truncation drops while this is not the case for the truncation after the second-order term (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: MINE increases the interpretability of the CNN model and classifies the transformations the model encapsulates according to their computational complexity.
source: In summary, MINE increases the interpretability of the CNN model and classifies the transformations the model encapsulates according to their computational complexity.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the analyses in Figure 2.

claim: Receptive fields compactly describe stimulus features that drive a neuron's response.
source: Receptive fields compactly describe stimulus features that drive a neuron's response (Dayan and Abbott, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience, supported by citation.

claim: Receptive fields reveal integration times and zero-crossings that indicate adapting responses.
source: They reveal integration times (those times over which coefficients of the receptive field are different from zero) and zero-crossings within the receptive field signal adapting responses that indicate that a neuron encodes the derivative of a stimulus across time (e.g. velocity encoding neurons) or that it detects edges across space.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience about receptive field interpretation.

claim: The Taylor expansion of the CNN is equivalent to the Volterra expansion of a system processing information across time.
source: Since the input to the CNN at the heart of MINE contains information about each predictor across time, the Taylor expansion introduced in the previous section (Figure 2A) is equivalent to the Volterra expansion of a system processing information across time equal to the history length of the CNN.
evidence: This is a mathematical inference based on the equivalence of Taylor and Volterra expansions.

claim: Both MINE and directly fitting the Volterra kernels yielded receptive fields nearly indistinguishable from the ground truth when using Gaussian white noise as input.
source: As expected, both MINE and directly fitting the Volterra kernels yielded receptive fields that were nearly indistinguishable from the ground truth (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Under naturalistic conditions with slowly varying stimuli, MINE still yielded well-fitting receptive fields.
source: Under these more naturalistic conditions, MINE still yielded well-fitting receptive fields (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: An ordinary regression fit of the Volterra kernels failed to recover the receptive fields under naturalistic conditions.
source: An ordinary regression fit of the Volterra kernels, on the other hand, failed to recover the receptive fields (Figure 3B), which is in line with the observation that ANNs form an efficient route to Volterra analysis (Wray and Green, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation data shown in Figure 3B and citation to prior work.

claim: For high penalties, the direct fit of the Volterra kernels using Ridge regression yielded receptive fields of almost comparable quality to MINE.
source: Indeed, for high penalties, the direct fit of the Volterra kernels yielded receptive fields of almost comparable quality to MINE (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The CNN model fit by MINE had slightly higher predictive power compared to the best-fit Volterra model.
source: The CNN model fit by MINE also had slightly higher predictive power compared to the best-fit Volterra model as indicated by higher correlations of predicted activity on a test dataset (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: MINE is a practical solution to extract receptive fields that yields high-quality receptive fields in addition to other information about the relationship between predictors and neural responses.
source: This is not to say that no other way could be found to extract the receptive fields, but it underlines the fact that MINE is a practical solution to this problem, which yields high-quality receptive fields in addition to other information about the relationship between predictors and neural responses.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the analyses in Figure 3.

claim: The effective degrees of freedom of the CNN model are <50 despite having nearly 14,000 parameters.
source: Interestingly, in spite of having nearly 14,000 parameters, the effective degrees of freedom of the CNN model are <50 and the Ridge regression models that are successful in identifying the receptive fields approach similar effective degrees of freedom (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1K.

claim: The effective degrees of freedom of the CNN are limited by the L1 penalty on the weights, the Dropout, and the limited number of training epochs.
source: In the case of the CNN used by MINE, the effective degrees of freedom are limited by the L1 penalty on the weights (sparsity constraint), the Dropout, and the limited number of training epochs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1L.

claim: MINE can recover the types of receptive fields of neurons that can be obtained with system identification approaches under a broader set of biologically relevant stimulus conditions.
source: Overall these results suggest that MINE can recover the types of receptive fields of neurons that can be obtained with system identification approaches under a broader set of biologically relevant stimulus conditions.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the analyses in Figure 3.

claim: There is a high correlation between the change in output of the Taylor expansion and the true change in network output across the ground-truth dataset.
source: Across our ground-truth dataset, we find a high correlation between the change in output of the Taylor expansion and the true change in network output (Figure 4B, left panel), indicating that the local expansions using first- and second-order derivatives sufficiently capture the relationship between predictors and neural activity.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The Taylor metric correctly identifies the contributing predictors and their interactions on the ground-truth dataset.
source: On our ground-truth dataset, the Taylor metric correctly identifies the contributing predictors and their interactions.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: Sorting individual terms by the Taylor metric consistently ranks those expected to contribute higher than those that should not.
source: Sorting individual terms by this metric consistently ranks those that we expect to contribute (Figure 4C–E, red bars) higher than those that should not (Figure 4C–E, blue bars).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: MINE allows for flexible analysis of the relationship between measured quantities and neural activity.
source: In summary, MINE allows for flexible analysis of the relationship between measured quantities such as stimuli, behaviors, or internal states and neural activity.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the analyses throughout the manuscript.

claim: MINE approximates the functional form that relates predictors to neural activity and subsequently discovers this functional form.
source: The flexibility comes from MINE turning analysis on its head: instead of predefining a model, MINE approximates the functional form that relates predictors to neural activity and subsequently discovers this functional form.
evidence: This is a summary of the MINE approach.

claim: MINE does not make any assumptions about the probability distribution or functional form underlying the data it models.
source: This is possible since MINE does not make any assumptions about the probability distribution or functional form underlying the data it models.
evidence: This is a characterization of the MINE approach.

claim: MINE identified more neurons than regression approaches on the zebrafish dataset.
source: This allows MINE to identify more neurons than regression approaches on our zebrafish dataset (Figure 6D) while doing so in a less biased manner.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The regression approach especially failed on stimulus-driven units, leading to an overrepresentation of behavior-related activity.
source: The regression approach especially failed on stimulus-driven units, leading to an overrepresentation of behavior-related activity (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The linear model identified neurons belonging to each receptive field cluster.
source: Testing how many neurons in our receptive field clusters were also identified by the linear model (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D) revealed that the linear model identified neurons belonging to each cluster.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison data shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: MINE increases sensitivity for identifying neurons.
source: This argues that MINE increases sensitivity for identifying neurons, but at this level of analysis MINE did not necessarily identify functional types that were entirely missed by the linear model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison data.

claim: In four receptive field clusters, the linear model identified less than five neurons, meaning the cluster would have been missed entirely when using the linear model.
source: However, in four clusters the linear model identified less than five neurons. This effectively means that the cluster would have been missed entirely when using the linear model data as the base for analysis.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Applying clustering on the neurons identified by the linear model only recovers 4 instead of the 15 unique receptive field clusters obtained with MINE.
source: Accordingly, applying our clustering on the neurons identified by the linear model only recovers 4 instead of the 15 unique receptive field clusters that are obtained with MINE.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison analysis.

claim: The fit CNN models the computation of upstream or downstream circuits of the neuron in question.
source: We propose that the fit CNN models the computation of upstream or downstream circuits of the neuron in question but we do not think or investigate whether it models the circuitry itself.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the interpretation of the CNN.

claim: Given the simplicity of the CNN used in MINE, it is unlikely to provide interesting details about the circuitry itself.
source: This could be investigated in the future, but given the simplicity of the CNN used in MINE it is unlikely to provide interesting details in this manner.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the limitations of the approach.

claim: MINE applied to the mouse cortical dataset identified >91% of all components per session on average.
source: On average, this led to the identification of >91% of all components per session (Figure 5C) on which Taylor metric and complexity were computed.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: MINE assigns low complexity to the majority of cortical components; only 3% of fit components have a linear approximation score <0.8.
source: Notably, MINE assigns low complexity to the majority of components; only 3% of fit components have a linear approximation score <0.8.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The relationships between predictors and neural activity in the cortical dataset are largely linear.
source: This means that the relationships between predictors and neural activity are largely linear (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the complexity analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The apparent linearity in the cortical dataset is likely caused by the low resolution of the data, where each component blends the activity of hundreds of thousands of neurons.
source: While this may seem surprising given the high nonlinearity of cortical processing, it is likely caused by the low resolution of the data. Each component blends the activity of hundreds of thousands of neurons. Averaging across many individual neurons that each may have their own nonlinear responses likely obfuscates nonlinear effects.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed linearity.

claim: Visual stimuli contribute most strongly to responses in visual cortical areas with the expected left-right asymmetry.
source: Specifically, visual stimuli are shown to contribute most strongly to responses in visual cortical areas with the expected left–right asymmetry (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by the Taylor metric mapping shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Cortical regions enhanced for whisking correspond very well to regions marked strongly with a whisk event kernel in Musall et al., 2019a.
source: At the same time, comparing visual sensory responses to whisk responses shows that cortical regions enhanced for whisking (Figure 5G) correspond very well to regions marked strongly with a whisk event kernel in Figure 2 of Musall et al., 2019a.
evidence: This is supported by the Taylor metric mapping shown in Figure 5G and comparison to published data.

claim: Instructed left and right grab events largely contribute to motor cortical regions with the expected left-right asymmetry.
source: Furthermore, instructed left and right grab events largely contribute to motor cortical regions, again with the expected left–right asymmetry (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by the Taylor metric mapping shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Receptive fields for left and right visual stimuli in contralateral brain regions are highly similar to each other.
source: Receptive fields for left and right visual stimuli in contralateral brain regions are highly similar to each other (Figure 5I, left).
evidence: This is supported by the receptive field clustering shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The excitatory effect in visual receptive fields is stronger than the inhibitory effect.
source: The excitatory effect is stronger than the inhibitory effect (larger coefficients in the positive receptive fields) and both are clearly biphasic.
evidence: This is supported by the receptive field analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The biphasic structure of visual receptive fields mimics the linear regression kernel in Musall et al., 2019a.
source: We note that this biphasic structure mimics the linear regression kernel in Figure 3b of Musall et al., 2019a.
evidence: This is a comparison to published data.

claim: Visual receptive fields have essentially zero weight after the current time, which is expected since future stimuli are unlikely to influence current neural activity.
source: The visual receptive fields have essentially zero weight after the current time, which is expected since future stimuli are unlikely to influence current neural activity.
evidence: This is an observation from the data with a logical explanation.

claim: The receptive fields of left and right grab neurons are much sharper than visual receptive fields, indicating that these neurons influence movement over short timescales.
source: The receptive fields of left and right grab neurons, on the other hand, are much sharper, indicating that these neurons influence movement over short timescales (Figure 5I, right).
evidence: This is an inference based on the receptive field analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Grab-related receptive fields contain coefficients different from baseline for up to 100 ms into the future, suggesting preparatory activity.
source: Furthermore, the grab-related receptive fields contain coefficients different from baseline for up to 100 ms into the future. This suggests preparatory activity, that is, that future movements are reflected in current neural activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the receptive field analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Temporal transformations of stimuli are a notable feature of how zebrafish process temperature information.
source: Temporal transformations of stimuli are a notable feature of how zebrafish process temperature information.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Neurons that compute the rate of change of the temperature stimulus have been identified in larval zebrafish.
source: In previous research, we identified neurons and centers in the larval zebrafish brain that process temperature: specifically, neurons that compute the rate of change of the temperature stimulus (Haesemeyer et al., 2018) as well as neurons whose activity is consistent with integration of temperature fluctuations (Haesemeyer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Neurons whose activity is consistent with integration of temperature fluctuations have been identified in larval zebrafish.
source: In previous research, we identified neurons and centers in the larval zebrafish brain that process temperature: specifically, neurons that compute the rate of change of the temperature stimulus (Haesemeyer et al., 2018) as well as neurons whose activity is consistent with integration of temperature fluctuations (Haesemeyer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Simple regression-based approaches failed to identify neurons involved in temperature processing due to the nature of temporal transformations.
source: Due to the nature of these transformations, which were unknown a priori, simple regression-based approaches failed to identify neurons involved in temperature processing.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous approaches.

claim: Clustering was previously used to identify temperature processing neurons but precluded identifying neurons that integrate thermosensory stimuli and behavioral actions.
source: We therefore previously resorted to clustering to identify these neurons. However, because behavior is stochastic, one particular drawback of clustering was that it precluded identifying neurons that integrate thermosensory stimuli and behavioral actions.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous approaches.

claim: A total of 750 planes across 25 larval zebrafish were imaged, providing slightly more than fourfold coverage of the larval zebrafish brain.
source: We imaged a total of 750 planes across 25 larval zebrafish that expressed the nuclear calcium indicator H2B:GCaMP6s Freeman et al., 2014 in all neurons and the excitatory neuron marker vglut2a-mCherry Satou et al., 2013 in presumed glutamatergic neurons. This dataset provided slightly more than fourfold coverage of the larval zebrafish brain.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental dataset.

claim: 40% of the identified neurons were exclusively identified by MINE, indicating the superiority of the model-discovery approach.
source: 40% of these neurons, however, were exclusively identified by MINE (Figure 6D), indicating the superiority of the model-discovery approach.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: MINE consistently identifies more neurons regardless of the cutoff imposed on test data.
source: In fact, MINE consistently identifies more neurons regardless of the cutoff imposed on test data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: A total of 33 functional neuron classes were identified, all of which were identified across multiple fish.
source: In total, we identified 33 functional neuron classes all of which were identified across multiple fish (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The vast majority of reticulospinal neurons were classified by MINE to be driven by behavioral features.
source: As a control, we labeled reticulospinal neurons in six fish via spinal backfills and as expected the vast majority of these neurons were classified by MINE to be driven by behavioral features (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by the control data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Multiple functional classes of neurons with mixed selectivity were identified across the brain.
source: Across the brain, we identified multiple functional classes of neurons with mixed selectivity, that is, neurons with activity jointly driven by the temperature stimulus and behavioral outputs (Figure 6E, blue filled bars).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Mixed-selectivity neurons mark a previously unidentified class of neurons in the thermoregulatory circuit that might play a key role in behavioral thermoregulation.
source: These mark a previously unidentified class of neurons in the thermoregulatory circuit that might play a key role in behavioral thermoregulation: they could allow the animal to relate behavioral output to temperature changes and thereby characterize the thermal landscape.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional role of the identified neurons.

claim: Stimulus-, Behavior- and Mixed-selectivity neurons are generally broadly distributed but enriched in specific brain regions.
source: While Stimulus-, Behavior- and Mixed-selectivity neurons are generally broadly distributed, they are enriched in specific brain regions (Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G-I).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical analysis shown in Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G-I.

claim: Stimulus-driven neurons are enriched in telencephalic regions, as well as the habenula and its output region the interpeduncular nucleus.
source: We found stimulus-driven neurons to be enriched in telencephalic regions, as well as the habenula and its output region the interpeduncular nucleus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Behavior-driven neurons are enriched in hindbrain regions and the midbrain nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus.
source: As expected, behavior-driven neurons are enriched in hindbrain regions and the midbrain nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H; Severi et al., 2014; Thiele et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1H and citations.

claim: Mixed-selectivity neurons are strongly enriched in the raphe superior as well as the caudal hypothalamus and the torus longitudinalis.
source: Mixed-selectivity neurons occupy some regions shared with stimulus-driven neurons such as telencephalic area M4 and the interpeduncular nucleus but are also strongly enriched in the raphe superior as well as the caudal hypothalamus and the torus longitudinalis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Temperature-sensitive neurons were found in a medial zone of the olfactory epithelium.
source: Our current dataset did not cover sensory ganglia well (especially not the trigeminal ganglion) with the exception of the olfactory epithelium where we found temperature-sensitive neurons in a medial zone (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1I.

claim: The finding of temperature-sensitive neurons in the olfactory epithelium is in line with reports in mice and frogs.
source: This is in line with reports in mice and frogs that describe specific thermosensitive neurons in the olfactory epithelium of these species (Schmid et al., 2010; Kludt et al., 2015; Fleischer, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies in other species.

claim: Functional cell types identified by MINE segregate spatially within the brain, likely forming organizational units within the thermoregulatory circuit.
source: Overall these results demonstrate that functional cell types identified by MINE segregate spatially within the brain, likely forming organizational units within the thermoregulatory circuit.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the anatomical analyses.

claim: Analyzing brain regions for enrichment of encoding different behavioral features suggests a segregation in the control of swim starts, swim speed (vigor), and turn angle (directionality).
source: Analyzing brain regions for enrichment of encoding different behavioral features suggests a segregation in the control of swim starts, swim speed (vigor), and turn angle (directionality).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical analysis shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Swim start neurons are enriched in the dorsal thalamus as well as the medial hindbrain.
source: Swim start neurons are enriched in the dorsal thalamus as well as the medial hindbrain, while the ventral thalamus, the forebrain, and the locus coeruleus preferentially encode swim speed (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical analysis shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The ventral thalamus, the forebrain, and the locus coeruleus preferentially encode swim speed.
source: Swim start neurons are enriched in the dorsal thalamus as well as the medial hindbrain, while the ventral thalamus, the forebrain, and the locus coeruleus preferentially encode swim speed (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical analysis shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Neurons that encode turning are enriched in mid- and hindbrain regions.
source: Neurons that encode turning are enriched in mid- and hindbrain regions (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical analysis shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Neurons encoding behavioral features could be involved in controlling these features or alternatively maintain efference copies of the motor commands for other purposes.
source: Notably, these neurons could be involved in controlling these behavioral features or alternatively maintain efference copies of the motor commands for other purposes (Odstrcil et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional role of the neurons, supported by citation.

claim: Clustering of temperature encoding neurons according to receptive fields resulted in 15 clusters, with neurons from at least 15 fish in each cluster.
source: A clustering approach based on the cosine similarity of receptive fields (see 'Methods') resulted in 15 clusters. For each of these clusters, neurons came from at least 15 fish across our dataset.
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Each receptive field cluster represents a functional neuron class that extracts specific features of the temperature stimulus.
source: Each cluster represents a functional neuron class that extracts specific features of the temperature stimulus (Figure 7B, left).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the clustering results shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Clusters 1 and 4 are enriched in the forebrain and are most responsive to heating and cooling stimuli over slow timescales, respectively.
source: Clusters 1 and 4 are enriched in the forebrain (Figure 7B, right), and their receptive fields suggest that they are most responsive to heating and cooling stimuli over slow timescales, respectively (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical and receptive field analysis shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: Cluster 3 computes the rate of heating over shorter timescales and is almost exclusively localized to the hindbrain.
source: Cluster 3, on the other hand, computes the rate of heating over shorter timescales (Figure 7C) and is almost exclusively localized to the hindbrain (Figure 7B, right).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical and receptive field analysis shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: Cluster 12 represents neurons that are excited by colder temperatures and is found predominantly in hind- and midbrain regions.
source: Cluster 12 represents neurons that are excited by colder temperatures since the receptive field exclusively has negative coefficients (Figure 7C). This neuron type is found predominantly in hind- and midbrain regions (Figure 7B, right).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical and receptive field analysis shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: Some receptive fields have the largest departures from 0 at the start and end, which might indicate that the chosen history length (10 s) is too short.
source: We note that some of the uncovered receptive fields (e.g. clusters 1 and 4) have the largest departures from 0 at the start and end of the receptive fields. This might indicate that the chosen history length (here 10  s) is too short and does not cover the entire timescale of processing, which could be a result of the rather slow nuclear calcium indicator we chose for this study.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a potential limitation of the analysis.

claim: Mixed-selectivity neurons could provide zebrafish with important information about the thermal environment such as the slope of temperature gradients.
source: Mixed-selectivity neurons could provide zebrafish with important information about the thermal environment such as the slope of temperature gradients the fish can use to thermoregulate.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional role of mixed-selectivity neurons.

claim: Clustering of nonlinear mixed-selectivity neurons according to response landscapes revealed diverse modes of integration across 10 clusters.
source: Clustering neurons according to these response landscapes (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E) revealed diverse modes of integration across 10 clusters.
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Some mixed-selectivity neurons appear to add behavioral inputs linearly with thermosensory inputs.
source: Some neurons appear to add behavioral inputs linearly with thermosensory inputs (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E, clusters 8 and 9).
evidence: This is supported by the response landscape analysis shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Some mixed-selectivity neurons show gating, where swim drive effectively scales the sensory responsiveness.
source: Other neurons, however, show gating (Figure 7D, left, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E, clusters 0 and 1). Here swim drive effectively scales the sensory responsiveness.
evidence: This is supported by the response landscape analysis shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Gating neurons could act as coincidence detectors that inform larval zebrafish that temperature changes are linked to behavior as expected in a temperature gradient.
source: These neurons could therefore act as coincidence detectors that inform larval zebrafish that temperature changes are linked to behavior as expected in a temperature gradient.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional role of gating neurons.

claim: A cluster of neurons displays complex integration of sensory and motor information, with asymmetric response to temperature depending on swim drive.
source: We also found a cluster of neurons that display more complex integration of sensory and motor information (Figure 7D, right). At lower-than-average swim drive, these neurons symmetrically respond to both low and high sensory drive. However, at high swim drive, the response to positive sensory drive is enhanced, making the response of the neuron to temperature asymmetric in this regime.
evidence: This is supported by the response landscape analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Complexity is mapped onto both functional and anatomical features, indicating that this division is meaningful.
source: We found that complexity is mapped onto both functional (Figure 7E) and anatomical features (Figure 7F), indicating that this division is not arbitrary but rather indicates a meaningful difference in neuron function.
evidence: This is supported by the complexity analysis shown in Figure 7E and 7F.

claim: Three receptive field clusters have lower complexity than expected, indicating that most neurons in these clusters have responses that linearly depend on the temperature stimulus.
source: Specifically, averaging the complexity score for different receptive field clusters reveals that three of these clusters have lower complexity than expected, indicating that most neurons in these clusters have responses that linearly depend on the temperature stimulus (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by the complexity analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Cluster 6 had an average complexity score >1, indicating that the majority of neurons in this cluster compute highly nonlinear transformations of the stimulus.
source: One cluster (cluster 6) had an average complexity score >1, indicating that the majority of neurons in this cluster compute highly nonlinear transformations of the stimulus.
evidence: This is supported by the complexity analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Within the hindbrain, neurons of complexity class 2 are found medially in rhombomeres 1 and 2.
source: Within the hindbrain, neurons of complexity class 2 are found medially in rhombomeres 1 and 2.
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical clustering shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Neurons in the medial hindbrain region carry little information about ongoing behavior, which might indicate that they process thermosensory stimuli for other functions.
source: We previously found that neurons in this region carry little information about ongoing behavior, which might indicate that they process thermosensory stimuli for other functions (Haesemeyer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and is a speculative statement.

claim: Prominent clusters of complexity 2 neurons can be found in the habenula and dorsal telencephalon, consistent with the idea that these structures are involved in higher-order computations.
source: Prominent clusters of complexity 2 neurons can also be found in the habenula and dorsal telencephalon consistent with the idea that these structures are involved in higher-order computations rather than the short-time control of thermoregulatory behaviors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical clustering shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Linear neurons are enriched in the posterior and medial hindbrain.
source: Linear neurons, on the other hand, are enriched in the posterior and medial hindbrain.
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical clustering shown in Figure 7F.

claim: MINE has the potential to greatly aid the analysis of large-scale neural data.
source: In summary, these data reveal the power of MINE to identify computational features leading to a detailed classification of neurons into functional types. This automated, unbiased, and highly flexible analysis framework has the potential to greatly aid the analysis of large-scale neural data.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the results throughout the manuscript.

claim: MINE functionality is exposed through a simple Python interface.
source: To facilitate the adoption of MINE, we expose its functionality through a simple Python interface.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the software implementation.
